It's October, which means your inbox is about to fill up with Q4 planning advice. New goals, new funnels, new strategies you're apparently meant to start before the end of the year.

Before you add a single thing to your plan, I want you to look backwards. One of the biggest mistakes we make in business is treating every new quarter like a fresh start, when October is supposed to benefit from everything you built in September.

In this episode I'm unpacking why "just be consistent" is pretty useless advice on its own, the simple three-part check I use to find the real bottleneck in a business, and why your Q4 plan might actually get smaller once you do it.

Why "just be consistent" isn't enough to grow your business

You can be consistent at almost anything. You can consistently post on Instagram to the same 20 people. You can consistently send nurture emails without ever making an offer. You can record a podcast every week that nobody new is discovering, or keep creating new products while five perfectly good ones sit in your shop.

All of that earns a gold star for showing up.

But consistency amplifies whatever strategy you've chosen. If you've picked the wrong thing, you can be incredibly consistent and still wonder why nothing's changing.

So every now and then, stop asking whether you did the thing and ask what the thing actually did. Did it bring new people into your world? Did it deepen the relationship with the people already here? Did it create an opportunity for someone to buy? If the answer is none of the above, that's limited time you could be spending somewhere better.

Your business should have a memory

A lot of us run our businesses like they have amnesia. September ends, and we start October asking "okay, what now?" as if nothing happened.

That's the opposite of compounding. October should remember September. Q4 should remember Q3. And 2027 should remember everything you learnt in 2026.

Remember the email that got a ridiculous number of clicks. The offer that sold really well. The podcast topic that got more downloads than anything else. The collaboration that sent you hundreds of aligned subscribers. And remember the launch that flopped too, because there's information in that as well.

"I want to get better at using what I've already built."

So before you open Instagram to see what everyone else says your Q4 strategy should be, open your own numbers. Where did new people come from? What did they opt into, click on, buy and ignore? What took 15 hours and produced basically nothing, and what took an hour and somehow made $2,000? That beats seven marketing trends about someone else's business.

The three-part Q4 check: discovery, relationship and revenue

Consistency absolutely matters. You just want to point it at the right thing, and to find that thing, look at three areas.

Discovery: are enough new people finding you? So many business problems are traffic problems in disguise. "My offer isn't selling." Okay, how many people saw it? Discovery doesn't have to mean Instagram followers. Podcasts, collaborations, bundles, summits, Google and referrals all count. If hardly anyone new has entered your world in the last three months, that's your Q4 focus.

Relationship: are those people coming closer? Are they joining your list, opening, clicking, replying, coming to your events? If 10,000 people find you each month and 12 join your list, another 10,000 people won't fix it. Work out why the people already finding you aren't taking the next step. Maybe the messaging is unclear, or there are 17 options and nobody knows which to choose.

Revenue: are the people already here buying? If they open, click and tell you they love you but don't buy, look at how often you're making offers, whether they actually know what you sell, and how easy the path to purchase is. Last week's episode covers this.

Same problem, three completely different fixes

Imagine three business owners who all say, "I need more sales."

The first has 100 people seeing her content each month. Twenty join her list and two buy. Her conversion is actually fine. Not enough people are finding her.

The second has 10,000 people seeing her content, 50 joining her list and a couple buying. Her leak is the bridge between discovery and relationship.

The third has thousands of engaged subscribers who open, click and reply, but hardly anyone buys. She needs to look at her offer, her messaging and her sales rhythm.

Same complaint, three different Q4 strategies. Which is why one of the most useful things you can do this quarter is stop fixing the part of your business that isn't broken. If people convert well when they see your offer but hardly anyone sees it, please don't spend October rewriting your sales page.

How to plan Q4 around what's actually working

Before you set goals, pick content pillars or build a new funnel, sit down with your Q3 numbers and ask:

1. Discovery. Did enough people find me? Where did they come from? Which channels worked?

2. Relationship. Did those people subscribe, engage and stick around?

3. Revenue. Did enough of them buy? What sold, what didn't, and how often did I actually make an offer?

Then find the biggest leak and give it the majority of your attention, rather than spreading yourself evenly across all three.

Here's the nice part: your Q4 might get smaller. You might realise you just need to make more offers. No new channel, no new lead magnet required.

Then carry forward what worked. Use the email angle that landed again. Talk about a problem adjacent to your most popular episode. Collaborate again with the person who sent you brilliant subscribers. Rerun the launch that made money without exhausting you. Sell the offer people keep buying.

You're allowed to repeat yourself. The most successful businesses are often the boring ones that figured out what works and kept doing it. That's the kind of consistency worth committing to for the next three months.

Why an engaged email list isn't always a list that buys

Good open rates, clicks, replies, people telling you they love your emails. From an engagement point of view, those are brilliant signs. Gold star.

But enjoying your content and buying from you are two different behaviours, and it's easy to lump them together. "My open rate is good, people reply, so my email marketing is working."

Someone can adore your emails for three years and never give you a cent. They can learn from you, laugh at your stories, forward your emails to friends and recommend your podcast. All wonderful. None of it means they can answer three simple questions: What do you sell? Why would I want it? Why should I buy it now?

If one of the jobs of your email marketing is to generate revenue (and it should be, for all of us), those three questions matter just as much as your open rate.

Have you over-corrected on nurture?

A lot of us learned email marketing with the same rules: give value, build trust, don't sell too much, don't annoy people. None of that is bad advice.

But some of us have taken it so far that we're doing a fabulous job of nurturing and barely selling. A helpful tip. A story. The podcast. A free resource. Another helpful thing. Then six weeks later: "Surprise! Would you like to buy something?"

Here's one of the biggest giveaways. If your nurture emails sound like you, but the second you sell something you sound like a late night infomercial, there's too much separation between your nurture and your sales.

Your reader should feel like it's all one conversation. Here's what I believe. Here's the problem I help solve. Here's how I think about it. Here's what you can do yourself. And if you want my help doing it, here's the thing I have for that. That's useful, and it still sounds like you.

"People can't buy an offer you don't make."

Your subscribers probably don't know what you sell

This sounds ridiculous, but stay with me. You know every offer you have because you built them. You've stared at the sales pages, written the emails, set up the checkout.

Your subscriber has a job, kids, 84 unread emails, dinner to make and a school thing tomorrow they forgot about until 7:47pm. They are not keeping a mental catalogue of your products.

So if I asked one of your most engaged subscribers, "What's the next paid step with you?", would they know? If they wouldn't, that's a communication gap, and you can close it without creating anything new.

I've been looking at this in my own business. I have subscribers who engage with everything and have never bought a thing. Rather than reaching for my favourite coping mechanism (making a new offer), I asked myself whether I actually give these people enough chances to buy what I already have. Honestly? Probably not.

The weekly offer habit (and the maths behind it)

So I'm building a Friday sales email into my rhythm. That doesn't mean "Buy this, it's $27, click here" every week. It means Friday becomes a consistent chance to connect something happening in my audience's world to one of my paid solutions.

Some weeks it's a story. Some weeks it's a customer result, an objection, a seasonal moment or a product I haven't mentioned in three months. The format and the offer can change. The habit is what counts.

And by "make an offer" I mean actually asking. This is who it's for. This is the problem it solves. Here's what you get. Here's the link. You can be kind and direct at the same time.

The maths is simple. Sell once a month and you have 12 intentional chances for someone to buy each year. Make an offer every Friday and that becomes 52. You won't make a sale every week, and that's normal. But you've massively increased the number of moments where "I like her emails" can turn into "oh, I actually need this." You also get 52 pieces of data on what people click, which problems feel urgent and which objections keep coming up.

Your audience learns what to expect, too. When selling is a normal part of the relationship, nobody is shocked that a business owner has something to sell.

One honest caveat: a weekly offer won't fix everything. If the price doesn't match the perceived value, you're attracting the wrong people, there's friction in checkout or the problem isn't urgent enough, you'll need to look at the whole picture. But ask the simple question first.

By day three, I hated it. Five sales pages, a mountain of emails, and it was simply too much. Too much for me, and honestly, probably too much for my list too.
